title: Objective Morality
rootClaim: Objective moral facts exist independently of human beliefs, cultural conventions, or evolutionary history.

branches.text: Moral Realism: Core moral duties (e.g., prohibition of wanton torture of innocents) possess mind-independent truth conditions.

children.text: Convergence of Human Intuitions: Across disparate cultures and historical eras, core prohibitions against murder, betrayal, and unprovoked cruelty remain universally recognized.

Evolutionary Debunking Argument: Sharon Street demonstrates that human moral intuitions were selected for biological fitness and reproductive survival, not tracking mind-independent metaphysical truths.
Third-Factor Defense: Evolutionary pressures favored cognitive mechanisms that tracking objective environmental and social truths, aligning biological fitness with moral reality.
Darwinian Coincidence Problem: Claiming evolutionary survival selection coincidentally tracks abstract stance-independent moral facts requires an unprovable cosmic miracle.
Phenomenology of Moral Progress: Historical societal changes (e.g., abolition of slavery, civil rights) reflect genuine discovery of objective moral truths rather than mere preference shifts.

branches.text: Moral Anti-Realism & Constructivism: Moral statements are either subjective emotional expressions, social conventions, or systematic errors.

children.text: Mackie's Argument from Queerness: Objective moral properties would have to be metaphysically 'queer' entities unlike anything else in the natural universe, requiring a bizarre faculty of moral intuition.
Moral Naturalism: Moral facts supervene on physical and psychological well-being states (e.g., conscious suffering vs flourishing), requiring no supernatural entities.
Is-Ought Problem: David Hume's insight that no purely descriptive factual premises ('is') can logically entail a normative imperative ('ought').

Expressivism & Emotivism: Ayer and Blackburn argue that moral claims ('stealing is wrong') express affective emotional attitudes ('boo to stealing!') rather than propositions capable of being true or false.

definitions.description: The meta-ethical view that there are objective moral facts that are true independently of anyone's beliefs or attitudes.
An argument claiming that because evolutionary forces shaped our moral faculties for survival, our moral beliefs cannot track objective truth.
J.L. Mackie's argument that objective moral values would be metaphysically non-natural entities requiring an implausible mysterious perceptual faculty.
A relation where high-level properties (moral facts) depend completely on lower-level properties (physical states), such that moral facts cannot change without physical facts changing.
David Hume's claim that one cannot logically infer a normative statement about what 'ought' to be from a purely factual statement about what 'is'.
